newsitem.title: PERU: Risk of new mudslides hinders Peru disaster work.
newsitem.headline: Risk of new mudslides hinders Peru disaster work.

text.p: The risk of further mudslides hampered the search on Thursday for the bodies of 250 to 300 Peruvian peasants buried after an Andean mountainside collapsed and swept away two villages.
Distraught families sought desperately to identify the largely unrecognizable 41 bodies dug up so far by rescuers using picks, spades and their bare hands.
The few survivors of the tragedy told harrowing stories of the torrent of mud and rocks that crashed down on them before dawn on Tuesday.
Authorities believed many bodies would remain entombed as the 30-foot deep (10 metres) mud was expected to harden before they could be located.
"It is most likely that many bodies are not going to be retrieved," Civil Defence official and local Mayor Luis Barra Pacheco told Reuters.
The Civil Defence said it was flying in eight sniffer dogs to help locate bodies closest to the mud's surface.

Tuesday's mudslide buried the villages of Ccocha and Pumaranra in a remote mountainous region of southeastern Peru. A smaller landslide on Thursday morning covered the few remaining roofs of houses in Ccocha that had been poking out of the mud.
With clouds covering the zone at dawn on Thursday, Civil Defence officials feared rain would increase the risk of more mud slamming into scores of workers at the base of the slide.

In the central square of nearby Kerapata village, Civil Defence officials and forensic experts recorded details of the bodies brought in before sending them to a makeshift morgue in a schoolhouse in the neighbouring town of Tamburco.
A mass was to be held later on Thursday for the victims.

Dressed in mourning black, Dina Rivas Tapia stared up the hill from Kerapata's town square to the landslide, handkerchief in hand. "My entire family has disappeared. They were 25 people. I have no house, no money, I don't even have a bed."
The survivors spent Wednesday night sleeping under improvised canvas shelters and in government buildings in nearby villages.

Another survivor, Jose Saavedra, 40, managed to run out of the path of the mudslide before witnessing his home disappear. "It was all so quick," he said. "I just saw my house collapse with my family and I could not do anything ... the entire population has disappeared."
Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer warned of an epidemic of diseases among the 250 to 600 families left homeless by the mudslide.

After visiting the disaster site on Wednesday, President Alberto Fujimori flew on Thursday to villages in the northern region of San Martin. Amazon floodwaters from heavy rains there triggered a mudslide that destroyed the homes of 500 families. A woman and two children were swept away in the village of Yuracyacu.
There were reports of another 100 people missing in the isolated area.
In the central highland zones of Huancayo and Pasco, overflowing rivers and landslides killed another four people, with dozens of communities flooded and at least seven peasants missing.
